turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Ag, sorry we're late, Doc. The robot on Main Road was out and then the bakkie wouldn't turn over. Shame, I know you've been waiting.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. One second, this screen's frozen again. Sorry, say that again, something about the bakkie?
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ja, the traffic was hectic. His neighbour Piet had prostate cancer and he kept telling him he must come to the clinic. That's why we booked.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. I lost the thread while the computer was loading. Why are you actually here today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, it's not Piet, it's me. I'm getting up all night to pass water, the stream's weak, and I'm dribbling after. That's what's worrying me.
[SEG0006] person_4 (NURSE): Sister here. I did his vitals just now. Blood pressure one thirty eight over eighty four, pulse seventy two.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Seventy two, okay. Umm, how many times a night? Say it again, I clicked the wrong tab.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Three... no, four. Well, three to four times, mostly four, every night. It's been five months... ag, no, six months.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm his carer from the agency, I come evenings. I hear him up and down. Ag, and the load shedding last night was hectic, my shift got moved.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Six months. Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No blood. I've looked, hey, nothing red in the pan.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): And burning, or pain, when you pass water?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No burning and no pain. But Doc, is this cancer? Am I going to need an operation? I lie there worrying half the night.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't call it cancer from sitting here. Err, hold on, the cursor jumped. Which tablets are you actually on?

[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I've got high blood pressure. I take enalapril, ten milligrams every morning. I was on doxazosin too, two milligrams... no, four milligrams at night, but I stopped it in March. I was dizzy on it, but that's gone since I stopped.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He drinks tea in the evening as well, two or three mugs after supper. I keep telling him.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Two or three? Say that again, I was typing.
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two or three mugs of tea, after supper, every evening.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, that late tea will have you up. Any medicine allergies?

[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, no, no allergies. They offered me oxybutynin at the chemist but I never took it. I tried saw palmetto from the health shop, for a week... no, two weeks, then I stopped. It did nothing.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): So you never started the oxybutynin. Is the stream weak in the daytime as well? Any leaking when you cough or laugh?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Ja, it's weak in the day too, and I dribble in my underpants. No leaking when I cough. None of that.

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): This sounds like an enlarged prostate slowing the flow. That's only provisional until the tests come back. I'm sending a PSA blood test and a urine test, you can do both at the lab today.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): If the PSA is high, does that mean cancer? Will I need a biopsy? How long do the results take? I'm really frightened, hey.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): A high PSA is not cancer on its own. We'll go through the number when it's back. I want to start you on tamsulosin, four hundred micrograms at night, for the stream.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Tamsolusin? Will I get dizzy and fall in the passage, like with the doxazosin? And must I give the tea up for good?

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can drop the blood pressure a bit, so stand up slowly the first few nights. Cut the evening tea right down, you don't have to bin it forever. If you feel faint, skip the dose and phone the rooms.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll sort the tea, he forgets. Must I give that tablet with supper or at bedtime?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bedtime is fine. Sorry, the prescription screen is slow again. Come back in six weeks and we'll go over the results. Reception will book you.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks feels long. What if I can't pass water at all before then, or I see blood? Must I just wait? And will six weeks even show if the tablet works?

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you can't pass water, or there's blood, or you get a fever, come straight in, don't wait. Otherwise we'll see you in six weeks. The tamsulosin usually needs a few weeks to settle in.
[SEG0032] person_4 (NURSE): I'll walk you to the lab just now for the blood and the urine bottle. The forms are printing.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, sister. Oh, Doc, my father had prostate trouble as well, not cancer, just the enlargement. Does that run in the family?

spec.situation: Older man getting up three to four times at night, weak stream, dribbling; drinks tea in the evening; denies blood in urine; PSA and urine tests planned, tamsulosin discussed.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Patient reported weak urinary stream during the daytime as well, not just at night.
Patient denied leaking when laughing as well as when coughing; only leaking when coughing was recorded.
Patient was offered oxybutynin at the chemist but never took it.
Doctor advised taking tamsulosin at bedtime; caregiver specifically asked whether to give it with supper or at bedtime.
Doctor said a high PSA is not cancer on its own and they would review the result when it returns.

Doctor advised urgent review if the patient cannot pass urine, sees blood, or gets a fever; the recorded follow-up collapses this into a generic conditional consultation and misses the instruction to come straight in and not wait.
